hook.title: Team score vs personal rating
hook.text: A volleyball team has a **team score** and each player has a **personal rating**. Re-list the roster in any order: the team score must not change (**invariant**). The personal ratings must *follow their players* wherever they appear in the list (**equivariant**): the list of ratings is shuffled in exactly the same way as the roster.
hook.recall: Remember team score vs personal rating: graph → vector is invariant (same under reordering); graph → matrix (one row per node) is equivariant (rows reorder with the input).

explore.intro: Embeddings from one neighbour-averaging layer. Permute the input order and watch.
tasks: Find node C in the table after several permutations. Is its embedding ever different?
explore.takeaway: Invariant: $f(A_1,X_1)=f(A_2,X_2)$ (graph → $\mathbb R^d$). Equivariant: permute the input ⇒ the output matrix is permuted accordingly (graph → $\mathbb R^{|V|\times d}$). GNNs are built from such functions.

build.template: Mapping a graph to a **vector**: {0}.  Mapping a graph to a **matrix** with one row per node: {1}.

options: permutation invariant: permuting the input leaves the output unchanged
permutation equivariant: the output permutes accordingly
permutation invariant: permuting the input leaves the output unchanged
permutation equivariant: the output permutes accordingly

build.explanation: Slide 12: Permutation Invariant: map a graph to a vector; if we permute the input, output stays the same. Permutation Equivariant: map a graph to a matrix; if we permute the input, output permutes accordingly.

questions.prompt: A function mapping a graph to a vector is **permutation invariant** if:
options: Permuting the input leaves the output unchanged
Permuting the input permutes the output
It uses an adjacency matrix
It has no parameters
questions.explanation: Team score: roster order doesn’t matter.

questions.prompt: A function mapping a graph to an $|V|\times d$ matrix is **permutation equivariant** if:
options: The output never changes
Permuting the input permutes the output rows accordingly
The output has fewer rows
The output is the identity

questions.prompt: Which statement about GCNs is FALSE?
options: For a single node, averaging neighbours’ previous embeddings is permutation invariant
Considering all nodes, GCN computation is permutation equivariant
GNNs consist of multiple permutation equivariant/invariant functions
If we permute the input, the GCN output matrix stays exactly the same
questions.explanation: The output matrix is permuted accordingly (equivariant), not unchanged.

questions.prompt: Three nodes have embeddings with first components $1$, $3$, $2$. Sum pooling gives a graph-level vector. What is its first component after the nodes are listed in any other order?
questions.explanation: Addition is order-independent: $1+3+2=6$. Pooling makes an equivariant per-node output into an invariant graph-level output.

questions.prompt: *“GCN is permutation invariant, so after shuffling the input rows the output embedding matrix is identical row by row.”* What’s the error?
options: None
Per-node vectors are unchanged, but their *rows* move with the nodes: the matrix as a whole is equivariant, not invariant
GCN is neither
Shuffled rows destroy the graph
questions.explanation: Personal ratings are the same, but listed in the shuffled order.

questions.prompt: For a graph with $|V|$ nodes, how many order plans are there?
questions.explanation: Every permutation of the nodes is a different listing.
